items.title: She Tried to Live as a Man Before Detransitioning. Now, Her Story Is Part of a Powerful Book and Podcast Series
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Author Paul Hastings is on a mission to share powerful stories about “ordinary people” inspired by an “extraordinary God.”

In fact, that’s part of the title of his book, “Compelled: Ordinary People Extraordinary God,” a project that shares incredible testimonies of people who have gone from darkness to light, have faced difficult circumstances — and found freedom.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

Hastings, who hosts a podcast by the same name, said his mission to tell such powerful stories developed after years of working full-time in politics.

“I got really burned out, as you could imagine, just like the political cycle always, always on,” he said. “And so my wife and I just began praying like, ‘Lord, there are other things that you know I could do.’ And one thing that I was convicted about is that the whole time that I was in the political sphere, I had never once stopped to pray for my political opponents. I just cared about their personal destruction, which just sounds terrible, but I’m just being honest.”

This conviction led Hastings deeper into prayer, and he reflected on how God can change any heart, regardless of how terrible a person has behaved. This became the root of the “Compelled” podcast. The book simply builds upon that effort.

“The whole premise of the podcast, the radio show, and the book ‘Compelled’ is to find people with these amazing stories that their life truly exemplifies what it means to live a life compelled by Christ,” Hastings said. “So stories of stark transformation.”

He had to narrow over 100 stories down to just seven for the book, including everything from people who have been missionaries to cannibal tribes in Papua New Guinea to a mom who was falsely accused of murder and sentenced to life in prison.

“Each of these people has an amazing testimony … Christ just radically transformed who they are and how they lived,” Hastings said. “And trying to choose the top seven to place into our book was not an easy feat. That was probably one of the hardest tasks about the book, but hopefully we did a good job.”

Hastings said one of the stories that most stuck with him was Laura Perry Smalts, a woman who previously identified as transgender and lived for years as a man before finding Christ.

“When she was in her early 20s, she made a decision to reject everything that she’d ever been taught,” he said. “She thought that she would find answers by transgendering herself into a man. And so over the course of 10 years, she surgically removed every female organ from her body.”

Ultimately, after altering her body, going on testosterone, and growing a beard while living as an individual named “Jake,” Smalts changed her heart and mind.

“Today, Laura lives a completely different life than the one that she once lived,” he said, noting she has shared her testimony. “And it’s just an incredible testimony of the Lord’s goodness and kindness that no one is too far gone, that the Lord can save anybody in any type of circumstance.”

Ultimately, Hastings said he wants people to know it’s never too late to change.

“The Lord can save anybody,” he said. “So if you’ve got an aunt, an uncle, a child, and a cousin, a friend, a neighbor, and you think to yourself, ‘Man, this person is too far gone. They’re too far lost. They cannot be redeemed.’ That’s not true. … The Lord can take the most hardened sinner and transform their life.”

items.title: Do Prophets Still Exist? Meet the Filmmaker Who’s Investigating This Biblical Phenomenon
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Interesting.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Filmmaker Matthew Thayer is on a mission to explore whether modern-day prophets are still delivering important messages.

Thayer’s new film, “Can You Hear Me Now?” tackles this timeless topic, exploring whether the biblical dynamic of prophets delivering God’s Word to humanity is still alive and active today.

The film director said he “absolutely” believes God still speaks through prophets, explaining his perspective that individuals with this ability happened to “just kind of show up in the Bible.”

“There’s nothing that actually says, ‘Oh, this is what a prophet is,’ and so what that means to me is that the ancient Middle East — they were just there,” Thayer said of biblical prophets. “So the people of that era and the people that were originally receiving the words of the Bible originally just understood what a prophet was and a prophet’s function.”

The director believes it’s been proven that people have had dreams and experiences they can’t explain — sequences that tell them what will happen; Thayer said these are often quite accurate. He believes that’s because God has enabled them, through Him, to witness elements of the unseen realm.

When asked why some people in the church world might dismiss modern-day prophecy, Thayer held little back.

“Honestly, I think it’s because the dark spiritual forces that we war against, according to Ephesians 6, knew that communications with God was the first thing that they needed to take out,” he said. “Communications are taken out in warfare first … that’s just a standard warfare practice, and, so, if we are actually in a spiritual war, it would make sense that they would target prophets first.”

Thayer advocated being careful about the sources people gather their prophecy from, as false prophets can open people up to deception. Thus, discernment is key.

“To me, it’s more about who the prophet is pointing to,” he said. “Because that’s what Deuteronomy 13 very clearly stipulates … that there’s going to be false prophets and they’re going to be accurate. But if they’re pointing you away from Yahweh, if they’re pointing you away from God, then they’re a false prophet.”

Thayer understands some of the hesitation people have surrounding prophecy, explaining that his own skepticism came when politics and prophecy collided. He said it felt like some of those making proclamations — especially surrounding President Donald Trump in 2016 — felt like they didn’t quite land. But, over time, the volume of so-called “words” surrounding Trump shocked him.

“The amount of words that were coming out just kind of made me go, like, ‘I think God’s actually trying to do something,'” he said. “He’s trying to alert people to what’s going on and so that’s kind of one of the things that I was exploring with the documentary.”

Thayer recalled being in an auditorium in 2007, when faith leader Kim Clement offered up a prophecy many saw as predicting Trump’s presidency.

“We’re all standing there going like, ‘What? Like the apprentice guy? What?'” Thayer recalled, noting how Clement said Trump would be a trumpet. “Well, what does a trumpet do? A trumpet calls to attention, a trumpet calls people to action, and that’s actually really kind of very close to what [Trump’s] doing — like he’s pointing at things that we didn’t even know existed, and darkness, and corruption that was happening within our government.”

items.title: Other Strange Vocations: Grace in the Witness of the Saints
items.author: Mark Bradford
items.summary:
Mark Bradford

The question of how and to whom a vocation is given, recognized, received, and lived is where I want to go a bit further in this topic of “strange vocations” and disability.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Mark Bradford

I recently borrowed the phrase “strange vocations” in another essay. I had taken the term from Dr. Amy Richards’s book about inclusion of students with disabilities in classical schools, and she had discovered it in a treatise by St. Augustine. I adapted Dr. Richards’s use in that essay to support a recommendation from Notre Dame’s McGrath’s Center that men with autism and other developmental conditions be considered eligible for ordination. However, as Catholics know, ordination isn’t the only form of consecrated life in the Church, but unfortunately, there are few possibilities, if any, for men and women to serve the Church as religious sisters and brothers. I know a young woman who feels called to a life of prayer as a Carmelite nun, but she has been unsuccessful in finding a community that will consider her. 

This term “strange vocations” may be troublesome for some when used in reference to individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities. However, St. Augustine used the term miris vocationibus in his treatise On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, and the Baptism of Infants to develop an argument against the Pelagian denial of inherited sin and their reduction of infant baptism to a mere formality. In the course of his argument, he also dismisses the Platonist theory held by some of his contemporaries that souls exist before embodiment and receive bodies according to the merits of prior existence. But what does that have to do with disability and vocation?

Augustine gives an example of a man who was called a morio—a term we would now reject, equivalent to calling someone an idiot or simpleton. In his time, such a person would have been put on display for ridicule and amusement, but Augustine looked beyond the disability and recognized in him a deep Christian faith. In fact, Augustine’s point is that grace was given to this man more abundantly than to many of the sharpest minds he knew; he bore any injury to himself patiently, and he couldn’t tolerate anyone profaning the name of Christ. 

Augustine’s point invites us to reflect on our own attitudes toward those with intellectual disabilities. Rather than faulting one for their impairments, shouldn’t we be asking how God is calling this person through their impairment as a witness to grace—and allow ourselves to perceive how God’s grace is being revealed in or through them? The question of how and to whom a vocation is given, recognized, received, and lived is where I want to go a bit further than Augustine in this topic of “strange vocations” and disability. 

Actually, we don’t have to go any further than the witness of the saints to see how God’s grace acts within the lives of those with “strange vocations.” I’ll give three examples to illustrate the point, but there are far more than these in our Church’s rich history. 

St. Joseph of Cupertino (1603–1663) was born in southeastern Italy into a very poor family. His mother had been widowed after his birth, and the two lived together in destitution. Joseph was said to have been a burden to his mother. He was clumsy and profoundly absent minded and incapable of many daily tasks. When he was twenty, he was taken in as a servant in a Franciscan convent and managed to do menial tasks for them with cheerfulness and humility. It is said of him that he wandered around with his mouth hanging open most of the time and was given the nickname, “the gaper.” In spite of his strangeness, his Franciscan superiors recognized his deep piety and suggested he petition for the priesthood. During his formation, there was only one passage of Scripture (Lk 11:27) that he was able to expound on, and fortunately for him, this passage became his test to qualify for ordination. Joseph was sought out as a healer and confessor and for his reputation for levitating during prayer. Word of his holiness spread, and crowds gathered around him. These caused so much disruption that he had to be moved from monastery to monastery to avoid them. He died in 1663 and was canonized by Pope Clement XIII in 1767. 

St. André Bessette (1845-1937) was born near Montreal, Canada, and orphaned at twelve while still unable to read or write. He had numerous health issues and tried working at various jobs unsuccessfully. It is said that the bishop of Montreal intervened on his behalf with the Congregation of the Holy Cross. They admitted him and assigned him to answer the door—a position he retained for some forty years. He had a great devotion to St. Joseph and gave visitors who came to the door a medal and oil from the lamp that burned at St. Joseph’s altar in the church and encouraged them to pray. Stories of cures rapidly spread, and soon he came to be called the “miracle man,” with crowds gathering in long lines waiting to see him. He decided he wanted to build a small chapel to St. Joseph but had to agree to not accumulate any debt to do so. He began cutting the hair of boarding students at Notre-Dame College, charging five cents a head and keeping every nickel for St. Joseph. He also set out a small dish on the mountain beside a statue with a sign reading “Donations for St. Joseph” and took what pilgrims left. It took years to reach two hundred dollars, and, with the help of friends, he was able to purchase a small wooden shelter. That small shelter grew into a grand basilica that is still a pilgrimage site in Montreal. When André died, there were more than a million pilgrims who came to venerate his remains in the midst of a freezing Quebec winter.

St. Maria Bertilla Boscardin (1888–1922) offers another example of a vocation nearly lost because of other’s judgments. Born into a poor farming family in Italy, she was described as slow to learn and mocked as “the goose.” Some doubted that she was suited to religious life, but the Sisters of St. Dorothy in Vicenza accepted her, and she professed her vows in 1907. She went on to nurse children suffering from diphtheria and to care courageously for hospital patients during the First World War. At her canonization in 1961, Pope John XXIII praised the skill and quiet devotion she brought to her work. We can’t confirm that Maria Bertilla had an intellectual or developmental disability, but what her story teaches us is how the dismissive judgments and attitudes of others almost prohibited her from fulfilling her vocation as a religious sister. Her community’s willingness to receive her allowed a vocation to unfold that those judgments might otherwise have prevented.

Did these individuals’ perceived impairments obstruct their ability to live out their vocations in community? Hardly. The effectiveness of their prayers and the love they showed to others proved to their superiors their capacity for love and service. Can we not allow the witness of the saints to overcome our biases against men and women with disabilities serving the Church as consecrated religious? 

Along with the example of the woman who feels strongly called to a vocation as a contemplative nun, I also know of a young man with Down syndrome who has successfully found a place in a Benedictine community—but only because some of the men of that community had previously served religious sisters with Down syndrome in a convent in France. Rather than seeing this young man’s disability as an obstacle, they saw an opportunity to give him a chance to fulfill his vocation. To my knowledge, Les Petites Sœurs Disciples de l’Agneau, the Little Sisters Disciples of the Lamb, is the only place in the world where a community founded for persons with a disability exists. Why aren’t there more? 

This Latin word miris—as in Augustine’s miris vocationibus—can also be translated as wonderful, astonishing, or marvelous. Perhaps we need to allow ourselves to be astonished by deeply faithful men and women who believe they are called to religious life. Wouldn’t it be amazing if these vocations were no longer considered strange but wonderful instead?

items.title: Tuesday, September 29, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, today we celebrate the Feast of Saints Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Daniel 7:9-10, 13-14

As I watched,
thrones were set in place,
    and an Ancient One took his throne,
his clothing was white as snow,
    and the hair of his head like pure wool;
his throne was fiery flames,
    and its wheels were burning fire.
A stream of fire issued
    and flowed out from his presence.
A thousand thousands served him,
    and ten thousand times ten thousand stood attending him.
The court sat in judgment,
    and the books were opened.
As I watched in the night visions,
I saw one like a human being
    coming with the clouds of heaven.
And he came to the Ancient One
    and was presented before him.
To him was given dominion
    and glory and kingship,
that all peoples, nations, and languages
    should serve him.
His dominion is an everlasting dominion
    that shall not pass away,
and his kingship is one
    that shall never be destroyed.

Psalm
Psalm 138:1-2ab, 2cde-3, 4-5

I give you thanks, O Lord, with my whole heart;
    before the gods I sing your praise;
I bow down toward your holy temple
    and give thanks to your name for your steadfast love and your faithfulness;
    for you have exalted your name and your word
    above everything.
On the day I called, you answered me,
    you increased my strength of soul.
All the kings of the earth shall praise you, O Lord,
    for they have heard the words of your mouth.
They shall sing of the ways of the Lord,
    for great is the glory of the Lord.

Gospel Reading
John 1:47-51

When Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him, he said of him, “Here is truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit!” Nathanael asked him, “Where did you get to know me?” Jesus answered, “I saw you under the fig tree before Philip called you.” Nathanael replied, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!” Jesus answered, “Do you believe because I told you that I saw you under the fig tree? You will see greater things than these.” And he said to him, “Very truly, I tell you, you will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.”

Reflection

Friends, today we celebrate the Feast of Saints Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael. When the existence of God is widely doubted, it just seems unscientific to believe in spiritual beings. And yet, they are prominently mentioned in the Bible; they are amply discussed by the Church Fathers; and the Catechism of the Catholic Church boldly reaffirms the existence and activity of angels.

Do you remember how, a few years ago, there was an enormous interest in the culture in angels? One of my favorite stories had to do with a man who was flying a single-engine plane during a severe storm. At one point, his communication system failed, and he found himself without a means to make it to the airport.

Just as he was about to give up hope, a strong voice came through the radio. It gave directions to an airport the pilot knew nothing about. The voice guided him to the runway of a small airport. When he landed, he realized that the airport was abandoned. No personnel were on the ground or in the tower.

An accident? Or a sign that “there are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, than are dreamt of in your philosophy”?
